overview:
Kṣīṇa-kaṣāya (often written as kshina-kashaya) is a technical Jain doctrinal term that literally means “with passions destroyed” (kṣīṇa = destroyed, exhausted; kaṣāya = passions). It designates both a specific inner state of the soul and, more formally, the twelfth stage (dvādaśa-guṇasthāna) in the classical Jain schema of fourteen guṇasthānas, the progressive stages of spiritual development. At this point in the path, the soul has completely annihilated the four primary passions—anger (krodha), pride (māna), deceit (māyā), and greed (lobha)—in their operative form. The deluding (mohaniya) karmas that fuel these passions are destroyed, not merely suppressed, and therefore cannot re-arise. This marks a decisive transition from advanced ascetic purity to the threshold of omniscience.

In earlier stages, especially from the seventh to the tenth guṇasthāna, the aspirant progressively weakens and partially suppresses passions through vows, austerities, meditation, and vigilant self-restraint. The eleventh stage (upashānta-kaṣāya) is characterized by the temporary suppression (upaśama) of passions: they are rendered inactive but still exist in a latent form and can re-emerge if conditions change. By contrast, in kṣīṇa-kaṣāya the passions are fully eradicated through kṣaya (destruction) of the relevant mohaniya karmas. This distinction between suppression and destruction is central to Jain karmic theory: suppression can be reversed, while destruction is irreversible. Thus, the soul in kṣīṇa-kaṣāya has crossed a one-way threshold on the annihilation ladder (kṣapaka-śreṇi), making spiritual regression in terms of passions impossible.

From the standpoint of inner experience, kṣīṇa-kaṣāya is marked by a stable, unshakeable equanimity (samata) and complete freedom from attachment (rāga) and aversion (dveṣa). The aspirant’s conduct (cāritra) is perfectly aligned with right faith (samyag-darśana) and right knowledge (samyag-jñāna), and there is no residual tendency toward anger, ego, deceit, or greed even in subtle or unconscious forms. The soul’s vibratory activities (yoga) continue, and certain other karmas—such as those determining lifespan, body, and environment—may still be present, but they no longer arise in conjunction with passions. Because passions are the “sticky” forces that make karmic particles adhere to the soul, their destruction radically reduces new bondage and allows the remaining karmas to be shed in a relatively short span.

Doctrinally, kṣīṇa-kaṣāya is closely tied to the Jain analysis of bondage (bandha) and the five principal causes that must be overcome: false belief (mithyātva), non-restraint (avirati), negligence (pramāda), passions (kaṣāya), and vibratory activity (yoga). By the time the soul reaches the twelfth guṇasthāna, mithyātva, avirati, and pramāda have already been eliminated in earlier stages, and now kaṣāya is fully destroyed. Yoga persists until the thirteenth and fourteenth stages, when omniscience (kevala-jñāna) and final liberation (mokṣa) are attained. In this way, kṣīṇa-kaṣāya represents the culmination of ethical and ascetic discipline: the aspirant has not yet become an omniscient kevalin, but the inner enemies that obstruct omniscience have been definitively conquered.

Both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions affirm the centrality of kṣīṇa-kaṣāya, though they may differ in technical details of classification and terminology. Digambara texts like Gommatsāra and the Dhavala–Jaya-Dhavala–Mahā-Dhavala trilogy elaborate the gradations of passions and the mechanics of their destruction, while Śvetāmbara authorities such as Umāsvāti’s Tattvārtha-sūtra and Pūjyapāda’s Sarvārthasiddhi provide a systematic framework for the guṇasthānas and the role of kaṣāya in karmic bondage. Across these traditions, kṣīṇa-kaṣāya is consistently portrayed as a rare and exalted state, accessible only to highly advanced ascetics whose lives are characterized by rigorous vows, deep meditation, and unwavering non-violence.

In practical terms for lay followers, kṣīṇa-kaṣāya functions more as an ideal and a doctrinal reference point than as an expected attainment in ordinary life. It underscores the Jain emphasis on inner transformation: external austerities and rituals are meaningful only insofar as they contribute to the gradual weakening and eventual destruction of passions. Modern teachers often use the concept to highlight the difference between merely controlling anger or greed for a time and uprooting their karmic causes altogether. While the technical attainment of kṣīṇa-kaṣāya belongs to the advanced stages of the monastic path, its underlying message—that liberation requires the complete conquest of passions—shapes Jain ethics, pedagogy, and spiritual aspiration at every level.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha-sūtra (also called Mokṣa-śāstra)
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi (Śvetāmbara and Digambara traditions both revere this text)
primary_sources.translation: “From the destruction of the deluding karma there is destruction of the passions. When the passions are destroyed, there is the twelfth guṇasthāna.”
primary_sources.notes: This formulation summarizes the doctrinal link between the annihilation of mohaniya karma and the attainment of kṣīṇa-kaṣāya. The Tattvārtha-sūtra is a foundational Jain text accepted by both major sects. While different editions and commentaries vary slightly in wording, the core idea is that the twelfth guṇasthāna is defined by the complete destruction (kṣaya) of passions, distinguishing it from the eleventh stage where passions are only suppressed (upaśama).

primary_sources.title: Sarvārthasiddhi (commentary on Tattvārtha-sūtra)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Pūjyapāda (Digambara)
primary_sources.original_text: कषायक्षये कषीणकषायो नाम द्वादशो गुणस्थानविशेषः। तत्र सर्वे कषाया नाशं यान्ति, न पुनरुत्पद्यन्ते।
primary_sources.transliteration: kaṣāya-kṣaye kṣīṇa-kaṣāyo nāma dvādaśo guṇasthāna-viśeṣaḥ। tatra sarve kaṣāyā nāśaṃ yānti, na punar-utpadyante।
primary_sources.translation: “When the passions are destroyed, there is the special twelfth guṇasthāna called kṣīṇa-kaṣāya. There all passions come to destruction and do not arise again.”
primary_sources.notes: Sarvārthasiddhi is a classical Digambara commentary that elaborates the brief aphorisms of the Tattvārtha-sūtra. Here Pūjyapāda explicitly names the twelfth stage as kṣīṇa-kaṣāya and emphasizes the irreversibility of the destruction of passions. This passage clarifies that the term refers both to the state of the soul and to the formal stage in the guṇasthāna ladder.

primary_sources.title: Gommatsāra Jīva-kāṇḍa
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Nemicandra (Digambara)
primary_sources.original_text: सुखदुःखसुभहुसस्यं कर्मक्षेत्रं कृषति जीवस्य। संसारदूरमर्यादां तेन कषाय इति मां ब्रुवन्ति॥
primary_sources.transliteration: sukha-duḥkha-subahu-sasyaṃ karma-kṣetraṃ kṛṣati jīvasya। saṃsāra-dūra-maryādāṃ tena kaṣāya iti māṃ bruvanti॥
primary_sources.translation: “It ploughs the field of the soul’s karmas, yielding abundant crops of pleasure and pain and extending the boundary of saṃsāra; therefore they call it ‘passion’ (kaṣāya).”
primary_sources.notes: This verse defines kaṣāya by its function: passions ‘plough’ the karmic field, prolonging worldly existence and producing alternating pleasure and pain. Later sections of Gommatsāra, drawing on earlier works like Mahā-Dhavala, distinguish between suppressed and destroyed passions and describe the soul’s ascent on the annihilation ladder (kṣapaka-śreṇi). Kṣīṇa-kaṣāya is the stage where this ploughing activity ceases because the passions themselves have been annihilated.

primary_sources.title: Compendium of Jainism (Jain Academic Bowl Manual, based on traditional sources)
primary_sources.author: Modern compiled manual drawing from classical Jain texts
primary_sources.original_text: From stage 7 to stage 10, the soul purifies itself by progressively reducing passions (Kashayas)... Through such processes of purification, the soul begins to ascend on one of the two Srenis (ladders), either the Upasham Sreni (Suppression ladder) or the Kshapak Sreni (annihilation ladder)... Only Kshapak Sreni (Annihilation of Karma) can ensure complete liberation.
primary_sources.transliteration: English prose; no original Sanskrit/Prakrit line is given in the manual.
primary_sources.translation: English educational summary: it explains that the soul moves from partial reduction of passions to either their suppression or annihilation, and that only the annihilation path leads to full liberation.
primary_sources.notes: Although this is a modern educational text rather than a primary Sanskrit or Prakrit source, it synthesizes classical doctrine for students. It highlights the role of passions in the middle guṇasthānas and the distinction between the suppression ladder (upasham śreṇi) and the annihilation ladder (kṣapaka śreṇi). Kṣīṇa-kaṣāya corresponds to the stage where the soul has advanced on the annihilation ladder and destroyed passions, preparing for omniscience and liberation.

misconceptions.myth: Kṣīṇa-kaṣāya simply means that a person has good self-control over anger, pride, deceit, and greed.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain doctrine, kṣīṇa-kaṣāya does not refer to ordinary psychological self-control. It denotes the complete destruction (kṣaya) of the karmic causes of passions at the twelfth guṇasthāna. At this stage, the four primary passions cannot reappear in any form because the relevant mohaniya karmas have been annihilated. Temporary calmness or suppression of emotions, even if very strong, belongs to earlier stages and is classified as upashānta-kaṣāya, not kṣīṇa-kaṣāya.

misconceptions.myth: Once someone reaches kṣīṇa-kaṣāya, they are already fully liberated and have attained omniscience (kevala-jñāna).
misconceptions.reality: Kṣīṇa-kaṣāya is an advanced but still intermediate stage on the path. The soul has destroyed passions, but other karmas—such as those determining body, environment, and lifespan—remain. Omniscience arises at the thirteenth guṇasthāna, and final liberation at the fourteenth. Thus, kṣīṇa-kaṣāya is a crucial threshold that makes regression in terms of passions impossible, yet it is not identical with kevala-jñāna or mokṣa.

misconceptions.myth: Kṣīṇa-kaṣāya can be attained by laypeople through moderate ethical living and occasional austerities.
misconceptions.reality: Classical Jain texts present kṣīṇa-kaṣāya as a rare attainment of highly advanced ascetics who have undertaken rigorous vows, continuous meditation, and deep renunciation. While lay practice aims at reducing and softening passions, the complete destruction of their karmic roots is associated with the monastic path and the upper guṇasthānas. For lay followers, kṣīṇa-kaṣāya serves as an ideal illustrating the ultimate goal of conquering passions, rather than a typical or expected achievement in ordinary household life.

misconceptions.myth: The difference between upashānta-kaṣāya and kṣīṇa-kaṣāya is minor and mainly terminological.
misconceptions.reality: The distinction is doctrinally significant. Upashānta-kaṣāya involves the suppression (upaśama) of passions: they are inactive but still present in a latent form and can re-emerge. Kṣīṇa-kaṣāya involves their destruction (kṣaya): the karmic causes of passions are annihilated and cannot recur. This difference underlies the two ladders of spiritual ascent—suppression (upasham śreṇi) and annihilation (kṣapaka śreṇi)—and determines whether regression is possible. Only the annihilation path culminating in kṣīṇa-kaṣāya leads irreversibly toward omniscience and liberation.
